newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAFRICA COSATU SLAMS RESERVE BANK'S STANCE ON JOBS.
newsitem.headline: SAFRICA COSATU SLAMS RESERVE BANK'S STANCE ON JOBS.

text.p: The Reserve Bank's attack on proposed labour labour legislation underscored the urgent need for the central bank's restructuring, South Africa's largest labour federation said on Friday.

Backing up a similar statement by the ruling African National Congress earlier in the day, the Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) said the central bank's statement in its Quarterly Bulletin revealed the Bank's true agenda.

The bulletin, published late on Thursday, highlighted the inability of the economy to generate enough jobs to absorb South Africa's unemployed and went on to question the impact of the the Basic Conditions of Employment Bill, published in April.

The Bank said that implementation of proposals including a shorter working week, increased leave arrangements, a higher premium for overtime and a training levy could have an adverse impact on formal-sector employment.

"In siding with big business at such a critical point in the dispute on the legislation, the Reserve Bank has merely confirmed the general perception that, instead of being accountable to the needs of the South African people as a whole, they are only responsive to elements in business, particularly financial capital, who are also represented in their board," Cosatu said in a statement.
The labour federation held a one-day national stoppage to press its claims for a better deal for workers earlier this month and is currently threatening further action.
The ANC said earlier in the day that the Reserve Bank "which is supposed, constitutionally, to be independent, has no business whatsoever intervening in a biased way into this matter".
Cosatu said the Bank's opposition to the bill also underscored the urgent need for a fundamental shift in monetary policy.

"The effect of excessively high interest (rates) has been clearly seen: while the dividend of stability and development after the elections should have led to growth of at least six to eight percent, monetary policy has led to an actual contraction of the economy."
Cosatu said it planned to pursue the introduction of legislation which would lead to the creation of a more representative board at the Bank and a shift in the role of the Governor.
"This would lead to a Bank which is sensitive to the need to pursue policies which are in line with the development needs of the country."
